newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Moody's sees no threats from new NZ govt.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Moody's sees no threats from new NZ govt.

text.p: Ratings agency Moody's Investor Services said in a report released on Monday that New Zealand's economic fundamentals were solid, regardless of which of the two coalition groupings took power.

"Moody's believes that whatever the outcome of the political process -- the economic fundamentals of the country are solid and both major traditional parties are committed to the existing broad policy parameters," Moody's said in its in-depth analysis report about New Zealand released to clients.
"Policy modifications that can result from either coalition scenarios are not considered threats to the policy thrust already in place," Moody's said.

In the wake of the inconclusive October 13 election New Zealand's two major political parties, the ruling conservative National Party and the opposition Labour Party, have courted the New Zealand First Party in an attempt form a coalition government. Talks are still continuing.
Moody's said neither major party's budgetary programmes carried any real threat to sustained budgetary surpluses in the next few years.
"Having said that, vigilance will be required to ensure that the timing and scope of fiscal policy easing does not generate unwanted levels of stimulus to domestic demand," it said.
Moody's said New Zealand's external accounts should continue to perform much better in the current expansion than in previous business cycles.
A number of factors can be expected to support the external position of the country.
"For instance, an improved business climate has allowed New Zealand to finance a portion of its current account deficits through non-debt-creating inflows," Moody's said.
High levels of investment and industrial reforms had helped New Zealand's competitive position.
The Uruguay round of trade liberalisation would also help New Zealand more than most, Moody's said.
"In the short term however, New Zealand's exporters will have to adjust to a higher exchange rate environment," it said.

"Unless there are unexpected and fundamental changes in the medium-term policy orientation, it is likely that the New Zealand dollar will continue to show strength against the Australian and U.S. dollars -- a development that will force New Zealand exporters to maintain productivity enhancement efforts."
Moody's said it believed that both major parties seemed to be committed to maintaining large fiscal surpluses and the existing broad policy parameters.
"A Labour coaltion government may lead to more changes, such as a wider inflation target bank for monetary policy or some unwinding of labour market deregulation," it said.
"In general, however, modifications that can result from either coalition scenarios are not considered threats to the policy thrust already in place."
"It will be harder in the future to creat electoral majorities, so it will also be increasingly difficult to overturn legislated reforms already in place, such as the Fiscal Responsibility Act."
Moody's did not make any comment about New Zealand's sovereign debt rating in its report.
Moody's upgraded New Zealand's sovereign rating for foreign currency debt to Aa1 from Aa2 in February this year.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 373-1800
